review: With the exception of the antagonists, the main characters are extremely unlikable. Elise, a young factory worker who lives at a brothel, is an easily swayed idiot with a memory span of a goldfish. Then there’s Frederic, an aristocrat misogynist that uses every excuse under the sun to look down on everyone else. And finally, Franz, a well-off student that grew up among the upper class who eventually (after a series of misfortunate events) joins up with a group called Libertad. Franz is the only one that has any semblance of character development. He starts off naive about the world he truly lives in, but after being attacked by one of the bourgeoisie and being forced to live in poverty, his motivation for living changes drastically. The other two main characteristics remain static the whole time. Honestly, the writing bore me so much that I didn't even finish the main story line.

An Octave Higher, developed by Kidalang and published by PLAYISM, is a richly crafted visual novel that explores themes of social inequality, revolution, and the unifying power of music within a beautifully detailed world. Set in the city of Overture, a place marked by the stark contrast between a privileged upper class and the struggling Proles, the game immerses players in a society on the brink of transformation. The story revolves around three central characters: Elise, a factory worker whose love for music defies her harsh reality; Franz, a student of magical science caught between loyalty and curiosity; and Frederic, a revolutionary with a complex agenda. Their paths intertwine following a seemingly simple event—a broken piano—that becomes the catalyst for broader change and personal growth.

The gameplay in An Octave Higher is driven by narrative choices, allowing players to shape the story through decisions that affect both character relationships and the ultimate outcome of the plot. Dialogue and interactions are carefully written, revealing the depth of each character’s motivations and struggles. Elise’s resilience, Franz’s intellectual curiosity, and Frederic’s fervent revolutionary spirit each provide unique perspectives on the social and political tensions within Overture. These choices not only influence the narrative but also determine which of the multiple endings players will experience, encouraging thoughtful engagement and replayability.

Visually, the game excels in creating an immersive and emotionally resonant experience. Character designs are expressive and detailed, conveying personality and emotion through subtle visual cues, while the city of Overture is brought to life with lush, meticulously illustrated backgrounds. Each setting, from bustling urban streets to intimate workshop interiors, reflects the social divides and cultural richness of the world. The art is complemented by a carefully composed soundtrack that blends orchestral and ambient music, enhancing the emotional impact of key story moments and heightening the sense of immersion throughout the game.

While the narrative is compelling, An Octave Higher requires patience from its players. The story takes time to establish the world and its characters, with early chapters focused on building context and relationships before the plot’s full tension emerges. The branching paths and multiple endings, though rewarding, can be complex, necessitating careful attention to choices and consequences to fully appreciate the game’s depth. However, this meticulous design ensures that players are deeply invested in the story and feel a genuine impact from their decisions.

In summary, An Octave Higher is a thoughtful and engaging visual novel that successfully combines a rich narrative, complex characters, and immersive art and sound design. Its exploration of social disparity, personal ambition, and the transformative power of music creates a layered and emotionally compelling experience. While it demands focus and patience, the game rewards players with a story that is both meaningful and memorable, making it a standout title for fans of narrative-driven games seeking a carefully crafted and impactful journey.

Secondly, I don't know why liberals have such a hard time understanding this, but the difference between bourgeoisie and proletariat is not an amount of money, it's their relationship to work itself.

The bourgeoisie own businesses, and make money from the labor of their employees. The Proletariat perform labor to earn a wage. During the ending portion, when Elise is employed as a piano player she is still proletarian, same with Aretha. Hell even Franz is seemingly proletarian. Again, the distinction is owning or not owning a business.

As for other classes that make an appearance: Nobility (the Aristocrats) make money from taxing those who reside on their inherited property (land "lord"), and Lumpenproletariat (Amadeus, pretty much all members of Libertad, the beggars) are those who make money from crime or who can't make money because of a disability.

The distinction is the relationship to the means of production, not the amount of accumulated wealth.

Parting notes about Libertad: Any group that is Communist/Anarchist/Absurdist coded, while they certainly would have a resentment for the bourgeoisie, that is not going to be their primary motivation. The purpose of the "no god is comming to save you" talking point is to imply that we collectively as humanity must save and look out for each other as equals. It is a call to action, to be in solidarity with your fellow oppressed siblings, not just for blind rage against the universe.

Lastly, and this is another thing liberals never seem to understand, for Anarchist and Absurdist coded groups specifically, while they may believe in certain extreme actions, they by no means follow a policy of "the ends justify the means." Rather (and many expound upon this, like Emma Goldman) they believe in the idea of a "unity of means and ends" meaning that the means one uses to achieve an end must necessarily conform to the desired political outcome. This is why anarchists don't for vanguard parties like Marxists, because any such organization will necessarily be used to build the world that is created from the act. This is why anarchists (typically) do not employ indiscriminate violence (despite the medias attempts to portray it as otherwise) because anarchists do not seek to create a world built on arbitrary violent action. In fact, the absurdist view is that the only justified political violence is that which is done to protect the life or freedom of another fellow victim of the absurd.

To be honest, I'm not sure if I *can* recommend this visual novel. For once I wish there was an "inbetween" sort of thumb icon, because there's both good and bad here.

The good: 
The art is amazing, the magic system is surprisingly well-realized, there's a lot of interesting world building (when it isn't just pointless asides full of tell-don't-show loredumping) and I enjoyed how the story continually switches characters throughout the story, giving us a good insight into all three of them. Franz is  easily the most likeable of the three. Music is quite something to admire as well.

The bad:
Again, pointless loredumps. Also, without wishing to spoil, from a story centering around the possibility of fixing a broken piano with magic, at some point it does a complete one-eighty and becomes a humdrum YA novel story about a proletariat revolution that comes pretty much out of nowhere and makes you wonder what you just spent your whole playtime investing in. The revolution gets put down, the story ends, and you never even come back to the broken piano, making the ending very unsatisfying (then again, I've only played through once - it could be that other choices lead to an ending that's more fulfilling)

The two biggest problems in this visual novel are the two characters of Frederic and - especially - Elise. Frederic is just a bourgeosie ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who's completely unlikeable throughout the story, making it impossible for me to root for him. Elise is basically a mix between a manic pixie dreamgirl - who tries to talk a prole out of beating them up by telling him about dreams and rainbows - and a self-insert character who is so sweet and innocent it'll make your teeth ache. There's only one choice in the entire game where you can make her any less than angelic, and it doesn't *lead* anywhere. Which is a shame because we had a base for a really good, strong female character here.

So yeah, this is basically a YA visual novel - fun and engaging at a skin-deep level, with lots of spectacle and a seemingly deep message - but go any deeper and you'll find obvious flaws. I still recommend it for the art, the magic system, the world building and the music though, so consider this a halfway up, halfway down thumb.

[h1]A memorable game with simple choices[/h1]

I started An Octave Higher initially dubious it was ever going to entertain me, but by the end I was pleasantly surprised.

It starts out easy enough, but it has a strange way of swapping character perspectives so it can be a little disorienting to begin with. The 'story tellers' are Frederick, Franz and Elise, but Aretha is an important character as well. The story starts harmlessly enough but gradually builds up to themes of revolution, liberty, friendship.

Admittedly, it doesn't [i]look[/i] like a great game. The art is average, nothing really stands out about it, and there is no voice acting. But look at what it does do right - believable characters and story (even though magic exists), choices show a visual points guide in the corner showing how friendly the characters are with each other, and there are a couple of different endings (but not too many). 

As an added bonus, there isn't too much over-the-top girl-teases-boy rubbish to read through. Aretha does take the cake for teasing Franz though, but I feel like the writing has been tempered to keep the script enjoyable. Thank god. There is a bit of swearing as well but don't let it stop you from a decent story.

As magic takes a central role in the story, naturally magic combat enters into the equation. Magic takes the form of five elements (cliched, true, but I didn't care), with people typically only being strong in two of the five. Mana potions are a thing as well, otherwise no one can cast anything. Even though the game has choices, when it comes to magic combat you don't get any choice in what happens - all you can do is watch as characters single cast, or double cast, or combine elements, or nullify or amplify things. It can be entertaining but some of the ideas, and even some harmless dialogue seems to refer to other games or movies. Meteor being a myth from the past has a striking Final Fantasy VII vibe, for instance.

________

I think the relationship points system being visible is handy and makes replays for different endings less tedious. I got the true end first time, and I found most of the endings fairly easy to figure out. In hindsight it probably wasn't needed.

Nothing kinky about this VN either - no nudity or sex scenes. Just good storytelling. Recommended.

正直に言ってしまうと最初舐めていましたが、いざ蓋を開けてみたらめちゃくちゃ面白いファンタジーでした。たぶん見かけで損してますこのゲーム。

『An Octave Higher』の魅力についてですが、まず魔法に関する設定の作りこみが非常に凝っています。
例えば『An Octave Higher』の世界では空を飛ぶバスが登場しますが、ただ魔法で飛んでいるという描写ではなく、どういう原理で飛んでいるかまで説明があるのには普通に関心しました。
魔法が登場するお話は数あれど、その魔法の原理までを細かく作りこんでいるものは意外と少ない気がするので、こういうの好きな人にはたまらないと思います。
世界観の緻密さで言えばあの『fault』シリーズにも引けを取らないかも。

面白いと思ったのは、この世界は体内のマナを消費して魔法を行使しますが、マナは自然回復しないという点。マナポーションが無ければいずれ魔法が使えなくなってしまいますが、肝心のマナポーションは下級の労働者階級には手が届かない代物となっています。つまり貧富の差が同時に魔法の差にもなっています。この魔力の格差社会という構図は『An Octave Higher』の物語において重要なファクターとなっています。

[b] 気になった点 [/b] 
このゲームは3人の登場人物の視点から語られますが、1人だけクソ野郎がいます。主人公面してますがまじでクソです。嫌い過ぎてこいつの視点の話だけは読むのが苦痛でした。彼の脚本はもうちょっとどうにかならなかったのか...。Frederic、お前の事やぞ！

[b] その他 [/b] 
・プレイ時間は約19時間ほど
・選択肢ありのマルチエンディング(6個)
・対応言語は英語のみ
・単個数は12万語(文庫本1冊分)

[b] 総評 [/b] 
非常に重厚な魔法とファンタジーの世界が楽しめました。作風は少し古臭く感じるかもしれませんが、それ以上に読者を引き込む物語の魅力が本作にはあると思います。セール時は230円くらい(2023/2時点)で買えるので、ファンタジー・魔法が好きな人にオススメです。

TLDR: Disappointing.

I really wanted to like this game. The main thing I enjoyed about this game was its interesting magic system that also included science. The game had so much potential, and while there were some good moments in the story, an interesting steampunk world, and a great opening scene, there were some things I just couldn't overlook.

One of my issues was the innocence of Elise, one of the main characters. She willingly went along with everything with little consideration of any risk, and the amount of times she trusts male strangers is unbelievable (it's not like she isn't aware of the risk either, she even acknowledges this isn't a good idea at one point,but it happens to be maybe the fifth time she's already done it!). The second is the conflict between the classes in society. The whole main plot revolves around a revolution beginning by the proles, however Elise, a prole herself, is willingly accepted and sought after by two bourgeoisie and an aristocrat, and she willingly accepts them too. If there is truly that much angst between the classes to start a revolution, then why would these characters instantly behave like they are good friends?

Convenience of the plot at times was another. One or two convenient things happening I can overlook, but not this many. Plus I'm not sure why a highly decorated commander would readily allow young inexperienced students to help her qualified and powerful team infiltrate a rebel hideout and rescue the son of an important lord. Things like this that had no valid reasoning or explanation made the story less believable for me, and ultimately took me out of the experience and made it difficult to enjoy the story. Just to name a few things...

Other things to note:
- On my first play-through, I got the neutral ending with no achievement, which was disappointing. Some of the other endings are also very short, whereas others have a whole lot more story (maybe an hour's worth?) to conclude with, though these parts seem to drag on.
- The skip feature is also a bit tedious, with every image and sound still needing to be displayed, so it takes a while to replay to get all achievements.
- The story changes between three characters' perspectives, and sometimes this was a bit jarring.
- There are limited choices within the story.
- Sometimes it feels like there is an information dump happening and it can be a bit of a draining overload at times.
- I personally felt like the true ending was strange and disappointing. Also, the short part with the piano after the credits should have been great, but with no context on how that intriguing mystery was solved and whether there truly is more to magic than just science, it just made me feel even more disappointed with the story. It felt like several parts of the plot were never fully completed. 

I just wish this VN lived up to its potential, it would have been a nice breath of fresh air if it had. I don't think I'll be replaying it unfortunately.

First off, I will admit upfront that I did not complete a playthrough of this game.

That being said, I cannot recommend this game. I've played a number of Visual Novels in the past, and if I know one thing about VN's, it's that this is a story first and foremost. They live and die by their writing, for better or worse. And An Octave Higher is unfortunately the latter

This VN clearly has a really interesting, and well thought out world, with a magical system that has some intriguing depth. It is clear that a lot of time, effort, and love went into creating a logical yet fantastical world...

However, it makes the unfortunate mistake of being unable to contain it's excitement to tell you all about it in EXHAUSTING detail. There were far too many moments in the start of the game where this VN is more concerned with explaining, in depth, the logistics of any given topic than with actually progressing the story or having a scene that characterises the cast. 

It seems so preoccupied with preemptively answering questions on how certain modern conveniences exist in this world. I can't help but feel that the writers were hesitant to let too much of their world-building go to waste, and so front-load much of it in large, drab, boring paragraphs on how their magic system allows them to have flying machines and such.

While well-intentioned, I often found myself skimming and skipping dialogue. There are ways to make exposition and world-building provide character to the person speaking it, but this VN never feels like it does that.

I put up with it though. I was intrigued enough to see where it was going. But I ended up putting this game down for good when the character writing took a turn for the worse. I am no stranger to stories where the perspective character is not a good person. My favourite anime is Evangelion for goodness sake. An Octave Higher has one of the 3 main perspective characters as a morally dubious, and overall bad person. Which is fine. But what I took issue with was that I too often felt like the writing was trying to brush aside and downplay some of that character's more heinous actions in favour of making them feel more relatable. Perhaps that was just me, but I could never shake that feeling.

All in all, the combo of dry exposition and an improperly handled morally dubious perspective character was too much.

I won't say to avoid it, but I most certainly can't recommend it. There is not enough beyond its flaws to justify spending the time with it.

I came across this visual novel by chance in a recent sale, at a humongous discount. Needless to write I didn't think much of An Octave Higher at first glance, other than the premise looked intriguing. And boy, though it is not the pinnacle of this kind of game by comparison to other giants in the genre, it really is a hidden gem!

Without giving too much away about its story, An Octave Higher is about a group of characters who exist in a world of magic - which has also undergone significant industrial transformation. This has had various effects on people's lives, with how they respond to the problems they experience in this world being a major theme of the story. It is grounded in factual similarities to our world, that I think enhance it's appeal, to be a story which the reader can more easily relate to. It's no high fantasy tale, which is good if you don't like that kind of thing. The music being classical, another thread to the story, is also a nice change from more synthetic soundtracks. The art of the game, while not brilliantly dazzling, has a charm of its own which grew on me too.

Having written all that, I can't guarantee that you'll like every aspect of it. I particularly disliked one ending for being very 'tropey'. In fact, all the ends (even the true ending) made me wonder why the creators didn't expand more on the consequences of the choices made. Additionally, some of the writing is a bit crass, or the way language is used similar to modern ways of speaking (which isn't necessarily a bad thing) sort of takes away from complete immersion. However, I think that is part of the charm for this game which presents a believable enough setting for its story to successfully work in. 

Definitely recommended for visual novel lovers.

This Visual Novel took me on a ride that I thought would be enjoyable but because of all the issues that appeared, I decided not to continue on it. I feel that An Octave Higher shows a lot of promise but does not deliver. The start of it was alright and engaging. However, the writing and overall storytelling kept on bugging me.

There were places where information was dumped onto me, which is never a good sign for any type of writing. It would have been better to spread information out throughout instead of trying to hammer it in all at once. That way, it's more engaging rather than feeling like you're being force-fed content that may or may not be important to the overall plot of the story.

The switch between the three characters was confusing too and I can't say whether or not it added anything to the story. It's easier to focus on one character—as your main—and getting to know them as a person rather than more. It might have been better to let the player choose from whose perceptive they wanted to experience instead of the forced switch.

The text is what made me quit in the first place. It's highly inconsistent in so many different ways. It also had no character whatsoever, which means that it fell flat. The text kept telling me things instead of showing, which in writing is a sin. Many words were repeated when they didn't need to be and some parts made no sense at all. I had to look up certain terms, which I should not have had to do. One may think that using complicated words that mean simple things will make you appear smart, it actually has the opposite effect. It shows that the writer is naïve.

In the end, nothing was really memorable about An Octave Higher—unless you wanna count it for being unforgettably bad. If you want to play it though, then don't let my review stop you. Just don't be surprised if your experience turns sour.

Flaws with this game:
-The dialogue can get pretty boring or otherwise miss the mark. For example, it focuses on things like the minute details or alternatively, it simply doesn't give the important parts as much attention as they need. Or the writing tries to force certain words and phrases (mainly the magical related ones) into the dialogue, resulting in very stale writing at times. 


-The writing is inconsistent. Sometimes characters will act in a way which contradicts what they said or did a few sentences ago. Obviously, this can be pretty character breaking at times. 

-Writing simply doesn't make sense at times. It's illogical. The last criticism is part of it, but rather than just being two opposing ideas, the characters will also act in a very unnatural way; people simply do not react to situations and circumstances like this and it's very apparent. There is one spoilery instance in the True route where this is particularly true. 

-Choices(at least in the 1st half/most of the non-true ending routes) are meaningless in how they affect the the story and writing. What does this mean? It means you're basically playing the same story over and over again if you want to see all the endings and/or you don't want to use a guide to get the true ending. The choices only dictate what ending you get, not the scenes or dialogue beyond a couple sentences. It gets difficult to go through this visual novel after the first and perhaps second time. 

-On the previous note, how to get the true ending doesn't always make a lot of sense. First, it doesn't follow the same method which you use to get the other endings. Alright, no problem. That just means you have to go by the choices, right? Well, some choices to get the true ending make sense. Others don't. Or at least, as far as I can tell. I guess the biggest gripe as far as getting the true ending goes is there's nothing to hint or guide you towards it beyond a cryptic "...the end....or is it?" if you don't get the true ending.

-Speaking of the True end, wow. It's bad. Why? Because it ends literally after the final event is over. There is absolutely no epilogue. We have almost no idea what happens next. This is good because it opens the world of An Octave Higher for a sequel. This is bad because we have no idea what happens to the characters or world after. All are major cliffhangers and sort of cheapens much of the theme and events of the story since we don't even get to see a hint of the result. What's more insulting is another ending is actually better in some respects, mainly because we get some idea of what happens after the story ends. 

-World building is lacking in some areas. Many important parts of the world are unexplained as a result and leave some dialogue and actions feeling confusing, made up, incomplete or otherwise bad. Other parts of the story are simply not explored enough, which makes the world feel smaller and "flatter." 

-Some characters aren't explored as fully as they should've been. This leaves them feeling shallow, simple and makes the story feel like its missing something. 

-There are more than a few seriously important plot holes. It seems like many events, things, people,ect are discarded or tossed to the sidelines when it's convenient, never to be heard of in any meaningful way again.

A needlessly verbose Steampunk Fantasy world with lots of pomp but no originality, plagued by predictable characters and plot and an extremely repetitive narrative.

The story is told by the most part in the University of Overture in a default Steampunk/Fantasy scenario. It is told from the eyes of three different Cookie-Cuter characters: one standard arrogant aristocrat, one standard naive prole, and one standard enthusiast scholar. Their lives cross paths and then the story drags itself, mostly unenventufully, but sometimes interwining with your standard Aristocracy vs Prole plot. Regardless of which one is in focus, it is extremely verbose and slow-paced. Perhaps in the attempt to make you empahize with the characters, their thoughts and situations are repeated over and over and over and over and over and over. This is agravatted by the fact this is your default troupe and that you could have guessed their personalities right out.

The authors also sound constantly proud of their world building, which is annoying at times. The aesthetics are those of a Steampunk, but everything else is your standard Fantasy with people farting spells right and left. They seem to be proud of their magic system and keep explaining its intricacies - it honestly reminds me stuff I was doing for PnP when I was 13, nothing to be proud of and certainly nothing new. The combats are long, plagued by shonen-like dialogues and in the end the victor is whoever the author wants to be. Some exchanges are presumptuous and cringy e.g. "You're here discussing philosophical politics with a rebel," after a mundane exchange of words.

The background art is pretty good, the characters are for the most part good too, but sometimes the artist seems to forget to follow basic proportion rules (e.g. some of Gesang's images). The engine is good too, Linux port flawless, achievements also okay.

An Octave Higher presents a fairly Steam Punkish world in which magic and magic machines are the normal. Society is effectively divided between the nobility, the well off, and the poor laborers. Along side the story of a broken piano is how these classes both clash and cooperate. Likewise it is peppered with artifacts of how magic is studied in Overture (by scientists and engineers) and a variety of characters. It reminds me a fair bit of Bioshock Infinite's world but sprinkled with the skills of a math nerd rather than a history nerd.


The story revolves around three primary characters in order of introduction:

[list]
	[*]Frederic the son of the purse strings. Arrogant and aggressive how the story plays out rather determines how much of a bastard he is. I would say he brings anger to the equation.

	[*]Franz the magical scientist: who has been stuck with a thesis deemed impossible. He largely represents the average, decent human being in the story. The story unfolds with Frederic's funding of Franz's research and Elise's efforts to fix a broken piano with healing magic. I would say he brings reason to the equation.

	[*]Elise the kindly factory worker: roped into Franz's research. Being poor she lacks the math and science education of Franz but even she knows trying to fix the piano is probably crazy. But just the same she tries. I would say she brings compassion to the equation.
[/list]

Other characters are pretty much support: most of which are still significant. Like the world the characters get developed in enough depth to support the narrative without blasting us with dozens of extra paragraphs the way some novels might. Yet the supporting characters play quite a role themselves in how the story pans out.

Decisions influence the character's relationships and in turn how the story unfolds around them--such as the fate of the Libertad revolution. One play through is around 4~6 hours with some nice art and good classic music along the way.

Kinda looking forward to a sequel someday :D. One in which I hope the Dragoon's commander and the curious gentleman from the east will reappear.

Плюсы.
- Сюжет. Понятно, что у качественных визуальных новелл сюжет на первом месте и не может быть плохим, но мне особенно понравилось его разбиение на две большие арки со своими наборами концовок. Можно закончить игру раньше, выбрав, скажем так, слабую концовку (одну из четырех), а можно, сделав ряд правильных выборов, существенно поднять ставки и получить еще одну большую главу, насквозь пропитанную болью и драмой, с двумя сильными концовками, включая истинную (ачивка так и говорит).
- Музыка. Саундтрек состоит из двух дополняющих друг друга частей - бесплатной классической и авторской, причем авторские композиции звучат даже сильнее в рамках игрового процесса, а уж заглавная тема может спокойно исполняться оркестрами.
- Хотя самому игроку не дают погонять магические формулы и отводят роль наблюдателя, следить за баталиями глазами из участников не менее интересно, особенно за сражениями на ринге.
- Хотя в конечном счете можно назвать эту историю драмой промышленной революции, центральной темой является научное исследование, и меня очень радует показанная идея, что не все научные изыскания дают прорыв, иногда гипотеза является ложной (хотя истинная концовка дает какой-то мутный намек на то, что успех таки был достигнут).
- Также очень пришлась по душе попытка математизировать магию и связать ее с личностными чертами человека. Такого я не встречал ни в книгах, ни в кино, ни в других играх.
- Между делом самым отъявленным гикам могут прочесть короткую визуализированную лекцию по бинарной логике.

Минусы.

В общем, я всячески рекомендую данную игру за крепкий сюжет, выстроенную вселенную и ярких персонажей. К ней уже вышел приквел - One Small Fire at a Time, и я дождусь ближайшей распродажи, чтобы купить и его.

An Octave Higher tells the story of some people who can use magic within what is, for much of the game, an interesting setting. You switch between the perspectives of multiple characters (Frederic, Elise, and Franz) who occupy different positions within a stratified society that separates people according to their wealth. The wealthy and middle class have access to education, have less physically-demanding (or magically-demanding) jobs, and have much better lives in a general sense. The poor and impoverished are exploited in dangerous factories (the game's setting deliberately mirrors the disparities in wealth and well-being that existed during the industrial revolution), aren't protected by the police, are forced to live in areas more affected by polliution, and have a much poorer quality of life as a result of these and other factors.

Which makes it extremely disappointing that, near the end of the game, the narrative decides that it never intended to say anything interesting about the socioeconomic conditions of this society or the people in it. For the "true" end, the game shrugs and says "actually all violence is equally bad, no matter the circumstances. And it's unreasonable to judge political and economic systems as immoral, unjust, or violent (or any individual actors within those systems as such) because the intent of those systems (and actors) is more important than their actual effect on the people subject to the consequences of political decisions."

Everything goes back to the way it was. Maybe things will change some day, and people will stop being maimed in factories and dying on the streets. Maybe rich people will stop getting away with murdering anyone poorer than they are (yes, that's an actual plot point). An Octave Higher keeps setting itself up for a big climax that the game itself tells you isn't supposed to happen. Then it makes a really out of place Chrono Trigger reference, makes a pretty weird statement about martyrdom, and ends. Would not recommend.

[h1] In-Depth Thoughts [/h1]

An Octave Higher seems to take great inspiration from classic JRPGs in both its visuals and  the construction of its world. The outfits of characters and designs of items are most heavily inspired by this, along with the magic based on the four elements (and healing). Many of the ideas introduced serve as great thought experiments on how a fantasy world of this variety would exist. 

Political ideas are also contained in the story, mainly in the ideas of class struggle between the proletariat and bourgeoisie. Using Mana as the ultimate means of making a living is complicated by the fact that magic can more directly harm others, which is an interesting idea to play with. I'm not well-versed in political theory, so I can't accurately comment on how effectively these ideas are explained and presented, nor will I attempt to.

The affection mechanic that's implemented is not new to visual novels, but there's a surprising twist. [spoiler] While it is possible to simply get a happy ending scene between one of the girls and one of the guys, [/spoiler] this is clearly not the intended ending, especially with the (in my opinion, failed) joke ending if [spoiler] Frederic and Elise [/spoiler] have the highest affection with each other. If you have the option to [spoiler] fight Frederic [/spoiler] and choose it, you instead [spoiler] witness Franz lose his hands and start a revolution after a five year time jump. [/spoiler] From then on, the change in tone and feel of the game is a great subversion of expectations built up from the rest of the game.

Unfortunately, the dialogue is what hinders this game for me. The text is dense with characters simply explaining how the world works. Even internal monologues of characters completely familiar with the situations they go in great detail about the world solely for the benefit of the player. In around a two to three hour experience, you can have somewhere between nine and twelve choices total, many of which are solely for affection points and minimally affect the plot (if they do at all). There are only two choices that have a drastic affect in plot, and you need the first one to show up if you want to reach the second one. With the exception of [spoiler] Franz discussing how losing his arms affected his life and Jude taking him in [/spoiler] and some banter between Aretha and either Elise or Franz, the dialogue is either completely unnatural conversation or clearly there to explain the world to the player.

This over-explanation is particularly unfortunate when the writers decided to use subtle storytelling and the trope of Chekhov's gun to plant ideas for later use, as I took in so much information that twists didn't feel like moments of realization but took actual effort for me to realize that there was any setup before this. The most egregious case of this was the "true ending", which even after coming to a conclusion on why it happened, I'm still not sure if it's correct or even logically consistent with everything explained about this world. The only reason I can call it the "true ending" is because of the special end credits and that the achievement for this ending explicitly calls it such. Of all the endings, this one would be the most important to properly convey to the player, and it instead left me dumbfounded.

The art is pretty good, and the music is phenomenal (even if the looping sounds jarring), but it's not enough for me to enjoy this game.

[h1] TL:DR [/h1]

As interesting as the possible twists are and how they change the story, the long-winded and overly-explanatory dialogue made it difficult for me to enjoy An Octave Higher and made it difficult to recall the few subtle details necessary for such twists and plot points to make sense.
